title: Schnorr-like Signatures in the Non-Observable Random Oracle Model
abstract:
Schnorr's signature scheme and many of its variants are among the most efficient group-based digital signature schemes. Schnorr's scheme has very compact signatures (consisting of only two exponents in its most compact form). However, its security reduction is notoriously non-tight and requires a strong (“programmable”) version of the random oracle model. Variants with a tight(er) security proof in a more realistic model exist, but are less compact and efficient.

In this work, we investigate whether these disadvantages are inherent to Schnorr's signatures and its variants. In particular, we define a family of “Schnorr-like” signature schemes, which contains group-based signature schemes with verification similar to Schnorr's scheme. To explore the necessity of (heavy) random oracle abstractions for such schemes, we allow only for a very weak (“non-programmable, non-observable”) version of a random oracle in the security proof. Our main result is that there is no tight reduction of the security of any such “Schnorr-like” scheme to any group-based assumption that holds generically.

We also show that this result itself is tight, in the sense that non-tightly secure schemes exist. Similarly, already for a slightly generalized definition of “extended Schnorr-like” schemes, tightly secure schemes exist.

Our main result employs a meta-reduction with a new “filtering” technique that may be of independent interest.

1   Introduction

Schnorr signatures. Schnorr signatures [Sch90] are among the most compact and efficient group-
based digital signature schemes. They use a group in a black-box manner, except that group elements
are hashed to bitstrings at one point during signature generation and verification. Schnorr signatures
can be proven secure assuming one-wayness of exponentiation in the used group, but the known
proof only works in the programmable random oracle model [PS96, FH17]. Furthermore, this is
inherently non-tight, i.e., suffers from a large security loss [Seu12, FJS14].1 2 On the other hand,
variants of Schnorr’s scheme are even tightly secure in the so-called non-programmable random or-
acle model [FHJ20]. However, it is somewhat unsatisfying that the only known analyses of a highly
practical family of signatures schemes rely on a proof heuristic such as the random oracle methodology.

Random oracles, and how they differ. The random oracle model, introduced in complexity
theory [BG81], has proved to be a highly useful heuristic for security proofs [BR93]. In it, a hash
function OH used by a cryptographic scheme is modeled to be a truly random function in the security
analysis (although in practice, OH will have to be implemented by a concrete function such as SHA-3).
1
  Cryptographic reductions construct from any given adversary A on the investigated scheme a solver B for
  the underlying (presumably hard) computational problem. If B takes more resources or is less successful
  than A, then that reduction is called non-tight. Tight reductions are preferable from a concrete security
  standpoint.
2
  We remark that it is possible to prove Schnorr signatures even tightly (or “somewhat tightly” [BD20, RS21])
  secure, under an ad-hoc complexity assumption [CFO24] or in idealized models of (group) computa-
  tion [FKL18, FPS20].
Specifically, most known random oracle proofs assume that OH is observable [FLR+ 10, AB13] by the
security reduction R, i.e., that R sees what OH -queries an adversary makes. Many proofs also assume
that OH is programmable [BR93], i.e., that R can intercept adversarial OH -queries and answer them
arbitrarily.
    A proof in the non-observable (or non-programmable) random oracle model is always preferable to
one in the observable (or programmable) random oracle model. The fewer idealizations are necessary
for the analysis, the more realistic the derived security guarantees become. In particular for the case of
Schnorr signatures and its variants, the absence of security analyses (under standard assumptions) in
the non-observable random oracle may be considered a bit worrying. At least for unmodified Schnorr
signatures, we know that programmable random oracles are necessary [FJS14], and similar results
for other cryptographic schemes or tasks are known as well [Nie02, FLR+ 10]. But already for slight
variants of Schnorr signatures, it is unclear whether a proof in the non-observable random oracle
model exists.

Our definition of Schnorr-like signatures. To state our contribution, we formulate a class of
“Schnorr-like” signatures that generalizes Schnorr signatures.
   Recall that verification in the original Schnorr signature scheme works as follows: given public
key pk = (g0 , g1 ) (consisting of two group elements) and a signature σ = (h, t) (consisting of a group
element h and an exponent t) for a message m, verification is successful iff

                                           t · g0 − r · g1 = h,

where r = OH (m, h) is computed using the hash function OH . (Throughout the paper, we write the
group operation additively as above.)
    Schnorr-like signatures follow a similar, but more general, pattern: they are group-based (formal-
ized in a variant of Maurer’s generic group model [Mau05]), and they may utilize a hash function
OH that maps group elements to bitstrings. Verification may only check a single system of linear
equations
                                               A · g = h,
where g and h are vectors of group elements from public key and signature, respectively, and A is an
exponent matrix that may depend on the message, the signature, and a single hash value (derived
from public key and the signature).
    Beyond Schnorr signatures, many other schemes that follow the Fiat-Shamir paradigm can be
formalized in this way [FS87].3 However, unlike the negative results from e.g., [KMP16, FHJ20], we
do not require that the signature is derived from the Fiat-Shamir paradigm; we only require a certain
algebraic form.

Our results. Our main result is a lower bound:

(1) There is no tight security reduction of any Schnorr-like scheme to any computational assumption
    in the generic group model.

Our result relies on a new type of meta-reduction (that goes far beyond the techniques used in [FJS14]
for the unmodified Schnorr scheme): in our setting, the distribution of forgeries that a straightforward
(computationally unbounded) ideal adversary would produce differs significantly from the distribu-
tion that an efficient meta-reduction (who does not know the dlog of the public key elements g)
can simulate. We use what we call a “filtering” technique that, using just a few signature queries,
extracts information about sk and the reduction’s distribution of signatures. We then show that this
information implies some forgery distribution that both the ideal adversary and the meta-reduction
are able to adhere to if they have the filtering step built-in (see 2 for a technical overview).
     We also show that our main result is essentially optimal:

     does not require observable or programmable random oracles, but still suffices to show unforge-

(2b) We can also circumvent our main result by generalizing the class of Schnorr-like signatures
     slightly, to “extended Schnorr-like signatures”. Such signatures schemes are identical to Schnorr-
     like schemes, except that verification may be of the form

                                                  A · g = B · h,

2   Technical overview


We are interested in a computational model that is just expressive enough to construct secure (group-
based) signatures. We start by describing this model, consisting of a generic group and a random
oracle.

Generic group. We assume a generic group [Nec94, BL96, Sho97, Mau05, Zha22] in the formalization
of Maurer [Mau05].5 Intuitively, this means that every algorithm has access to an abstract prime-order
group, but only through explicit oracle queries (for group operation and equality tests).

    In Maurer’s formalization, there exist no binary representations of group elements. An algorithm
only gets a “reference” supplied by the group oracle for each group element that is operated on.
This reference is generally different for different users of the group oracle. This stands in contrast
to e.g. Shoup’s model [Sho97], where group elements have random encodings. The issue with such a
model is that the encodings yield a source of entropy and can be exploited to obtain an unlimited
random oracle functionality, hence immediately allowing to construct OWF-based signature schemes.
These subtleties are the reason why our result (in line with existing impossibility results on purely
group-based signatures [DHH+ 21, CFGG22]) are all based on Maurer’s model.

Random oracle. Since the group oracle alone is insufficient to construct secure signatures [DHH+ 21]
(see also [CFGG22, Theorem 3]), we additionally consider a random oracle. This means that all
algorithms have oracle access to a function OH that takes as input any combination of group elements
and bitstrings, and outputs a truly random bitstring. Because our goal is to find a meaningful dividing
line between secure and insecure signature schemes, we model OH in a very weak, non-programmable
and non-observable form. That means that a security reduction can neither influence (or “program”)
OH on particular inputs, nor even “see” inputs OH -queries made by an internally simulated adversary.6

Schnorr-like signatures. The “Schnorr-like” signature schemes we study have a restricted verifica-
tion procedure. Specifically, say (without loss of generality) that the public keys and signatures are
of the form pk = (g, s) and σ = (h, t), where g and h are vectors of group elements, and s and t are
arbitrary bitstrings. Then, we mandate that verification, on input pk, σ, and a (bitstring) message
m, consists of a single check of the form

                                         A(s, m, r, t) · g = h,                                      (1)

where r = OH (C(s, m, t) · h, f (s, m, t)), and A, C, and f are arbitrary (but fixed) functions. In other
words, verification makes only a (potentially large) number of non-adaptive group equality checks,
whose coefficients may involve the result r of a single hash query. We call such signatures “Schnorr-
like”, since Schnorr signatures are of this form.

    Note that (1) already allows to express the verification of non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs
derived from the Fiat-Shamir paradigm. This will be a great aid in our positive results.7 Still, our
lower bound will show that (1) is quite limiting, and we thus also define “extended Schnorr-type
signatures”, where
                                  A(s, m, r, t) · g = B(s, m, r, t) · h                           (2)
replaces form (1), using another arbitrary (but fixed) function B. We will exhibit an interesting
signature scheme with a verification of the form (2).

2.1     Impossibility of tightly secure Schnorr-like signature schemes

We start with an overview of the techniques used in our main result: the impossibility of Schnorr-like
signature schemes tightly reducible to any assumption that holds in the GGM. (See Section 5 for a
formal statement and proof.)


Meta-reduction strategy. Suppose there is some generic reduction R (treating the random oracle
as non-observable and non-programmable) that reduces EUF-CMA security of some Schnorr-like sig-
nature scheme Σ to an assumption that holds in the GGM. This means that for any generic (and
even unbounded8 ) adversary A that has non-negligible advantage in the EUF-CMA game, RA breaks
the underlying (generically true) assumption.
    Our impossibility result excludes the existence of such a reduction R. To this end, we will follow
the meta-reduction technique [Cor00]. This requires first defining some adversary A that has non-
negligible EUF-CMA advantage, which guarantees us that RA breaks the underlying assumption.
Second, we need to transform RA into a so-called meta-reduction M, and prove that M breaks the
assumption whenever RA does. The crucial point is that this argument does not require the adversary
A to be efficient: as long as the meta-reduction M is efficient, the assumption is broken and hence one
of the premises (i.e., existence of a reduction R or validity of the assumption itself) must be false.
    On a high level, we leverage the following idea: Recall that the reduction R must be non-
programming, i.e., it may only access the RO OH explicitly through some provided interface. This
interface is made available only to the reduction R and to the adversary A that R is interacting with.
Normally, the interface would just keep state of a uniformly random function, and answer all queries
from R and A accordingly. However, the meta-reduction M only needs to be an adversary against the
underlying assumption, which is a pure group-based assumption that is true in the GGM and cannot
refer to the RO in any way.
    Therefore, M entirely takes control of the random oracle, which we can use to our advantage: say
we first construct an unbounded adversary Aunbounded against EUF-CMA security, which accesses the
RO in the same way as reduction R. We know that RAunbounded (which, so far, makes a super-polynomially
number of group operations) breaks the underlying group assumption. Then, we can construct another
programming adversary Aprog against EUF-CMA, which has the capability to program the RO (but
is not unbounded anymore). Then, M := RAprog is a well-formed meta-reduction. As long as we show
that RAprog and RAunbounded behave statistically very close (including the behavior of the RO itself), then
we successfully broke the underlying assumption using RAprog . See Figure 3.
    We point out that [FHJ20] follows a similar high-level strategy to show that signature schemes
using “parallel-OR techniques” cannot be proven secure using a non-programming reduction R. They
also define a meta-reduction M that programs the ROM, but their techniques for constructing M are
entirely different from ours.
